title: Complexity and the Cost of Search: Visual Guide
outline: Title: Complexity and the Cost of Search: Visual Guide

1. Precompute Or Scan | a slider over how many lookups a system will serve against 1,000,000 records, pricing rescan vs sort-then-binary-search vs build-a-hash-map | DE 401's precompute vs compute-on-read decision is arithmetic: one lookup favours the O(n) scan, and the index only pays back across queries, with the crossover near twenty

2. Scan Search Or Probe | collection size dragged from 10 to 10,000,000 with a toggle that makes every hash key collide, plus per-method capability chips | linear scan is O(n) with no preconditions, binary search is O(log n) on sorted random access, and a hash probe is only EXPECTED O(1) — and each buys a different contract, so range and predicate questions decide the answer as often as the bound does

3. Two Cursors Stepping | a step-through of the two-cursor intersection of A=[2,4,8,16,32] and B=[1,2,8,9,32,40], with live advance counters against the m+n budget, and a second dataset of two identical lists | the O(m+n) bound is a proof by accounting — every iteration is charged to a cursor advance and no cursor moves backward — and intersection cost is not output cost, since ten million matches still cost Omega(10,000,000) to materialise

4. Skew Picks The Plan | the shorter list dragged from 1 to 10,000,000 against a fixed n=10,000,000, comparing m+n merge advances with m·log2(n) binary probes, plus a three-term query reordered between rarest-first and longest-two-first | which bound is smaller depends entirely on skew, and intersecting the rarest postings list first bounds every later step — which is why document frequency is a query-planning statistic

5. Bytes Or Latency | random lookups dragged from 1 to 100,000,000 against a 400 MB sequential scan, with a layout toggle that turns the contiguous array into pointer-chased linked-list nodes | sequential access beats random access by roughly 400-fold because hardware moves 64-byte blocks, but a 400 MB scan to find one key still loses to a cached index, and a bad layout destroys sequentiality without changing the algorithm
